323.title: The ones who carry it
323.hook: millions have memorized the whole Qur'an, many as children
323.howItsDone: Many Muslim children and adults memorize the Qur'an in dedicated schools and circles, reciting a new portion to a teacher each day and revising what they know; a hafiz often leads the long Ramadan night prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qira'at: the readings, passed down in chains of reciters. Your line was many voices, one text.

In a small room in Cairo, or Kano, or Karachi, or a converted storefront in Minneapolis, a boy of eleven stands before his teacher and a row of family. He recites. Not a surah: the whole Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, from memory, for hours, while the teacher follows along and listens for a single slip. When he finishes, his mother is crying. There's a word for what he has become.
screen: `A BOY OF ELEVEN STANDS UP.` → `THE WHOLE QUR'AN, FROM MEMORY.` → `HIS MOTHER IS CRYING.`

segments.voice: The word is hafiz; for a woman, hafizah. It comes from a root meaning to guard, to preserve, to keep, and that root is in the Qur'an itself. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Guardian there comes from the same root. In the tradition, the memorizers are part of how that guarding happens: the book is kept not only on paper but in people. Nobody keeps a count of them. Often they begin as children, in schools built for exactly this, a few lines at a time, reciting each day's new portion to a teacher and revising the old. The Qur'an seems made for it; its rhythm and rhyme hold together in the memory. It says of itself, in Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" The Prophet ﷺ spoke about those who carry it. A hadith says the one who recites skillfully will be with the noble, righteous scribes, the angels; and the one who recites with difficulty, stumbling over it, gets a double reward. Stumbling, and still going, counts twice. The title even reached poetry: tradition says the Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz took his name because he knew the Qur'an by heart. And it isn't finished when the last surah is learned. Keeping it is its own work. The Prophet compared it to a hobbled camel: tend it, or it slips away.
screen: `HAFIZ: ONE WHO GUARDS AND KEEPS` · `KEPT IN PEOPLE, OFTEN FROM CHILDHOOD` · `STUMBLING COUNTS TWICE` · `TEND IT, LIKE A HOBBLED CAMEL`

segments.voice: Choose one short verse you don't know yet: the second line of al-Ikhlas, Allahus-samad, is a gentle start, or any short line you'd like to keep. Say it five times slowly while looking at it, then five times with your eyes closed, and if you stumble, it counts. If you're here to learn about the path rather than to practice it, learn the verse's meaning by heart instead.
Hafiz. One who has memorized the whole Qur'an: literally a guardian, a keeper. For a woman, hafizah. Today's word.
Your line: carried by heart. One verse, kept and tended, is a real beginning. See you tomorrow.

324.title: Prostration verses
324.hook: places marked in the mushaf where the reciter prostrates
324.howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear one of the marked prostration verses, many make a single prostration on the spot, in prayer or outside it, and the whole congregation follows the imam when he does.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hafiz: the ones who keep the whole Qur'an by heart. Your line was carried by heart.

The imam is reciting, and the rows behind him stand still, listening. Then, mid-surah, without a word of warning, he goes down: forehead to the floor. The whole room goes with him. A few seconds later everyone rises, and the recitation carries on as if nothing happened. If you didn't know, you'd be left wondering what you'd missed. You missed a verse that bows.
screen: `MID-SURAH, HE GOES DOWN.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM GOES WITH HIM.` → `A VERSE THAT BOWS.`

segments.voice: Scattered through the Qur'an are places where the text itself speaks of bowing down: the angels, the stars and the trees, the prophets, the believers who fall down in prostration when the verses are recited to them. At such places the Prophet ﷺ would prostrate when he recited or heard them. It's called the prostration of recitation, and these are the sajdah verses. Sajdah means a single prostration, from the same root as masjid, a mosque: the place of prostration. How many are there? The schools of law count them differently, so the number on the page depends on whose list a copy follows. They also differ on whether it's required. The Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools treat it as a strongly encouraged sunnah; the Hanafi school holds it a duty, wajib, for the one who recites or hears it. In a printed mushaf the places are marked, often with a line over the key word and a sign in the margin. Bukhari tells how the Prophet once recited Surah an-Najm, prostrated at its end, and those with him prostrated too. A hadith in Muslim says that when a person prostrates at such a verse, Satan withdraws, weeping, because he was commanded to bow and refused. The last sajdah in the book closes Surah al-'Alaq, the surah of the first revelation. In Pickthall's words: "Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near (unto Allah)." Prostrate, and draw near. Another hadith in Muslim says it plainly: a servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating. There's even a surah named for it: Surah 32, as-Sajdah.
screen: `VERSES THAT SPEAK OF BOWING` · `THE SCHOOLS COUNT THEM DIFFERENTLY` · `MARKED IN THE MARGIN` · `PROSTRATE, AND DRAW NEAR`

segments.voice: If you pray, make one prostration, forehead to the floor, and stay there for a few breaths. If you don't, simply lower your head, or rest your forehead on your hands, and notice what changes when the highest part of you comes to the lowest point. If a mushaf is near, the mark in the margin at the last verse of al-'Alaq is the easiest one to find.
Sajdah. A prostration, and the verses of the Qur'an where the reciter goes down to the ground. Today's word.
Your line: bow where it bows. In the Qur'an, even the stars and the trees bow down. Day three hundred twenty-four, done.

325.title: The longest and the shortest
325.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Baqarah at home, in portions or in full, because of the hadith about the house where it is recited, and al-Kawthar is among the short surahs often recited in the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sajdah: the verses where the reciter goes down to the ground. Your line was bow where it bows.

Two surahs. One runs to two hundred and eighty-six verses, and reciting it aloud is an evening's work. The other you can say in the time it takes to tie your shoes, and a child can learn it in an afternoon. They sit near opposite ends of the book, the second surah and the hundred and eighth, and Muslims hold that both are equally the word of God.
screen: `AN EVENING'S WORK.` → `THE TIME IT TAKES TO TIE YOUR SHOES.` → `BOTH EQUALLY THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: The longest is al-Baqarah, the Cow, Surah 2. It's named for a story inside it: Musa telling his people to sacrifice a cow, and their endless questions stalling the command. It holds a great deal: the story of Adam, the turning of the prayer toward Mecca, fasting in Ramadan, pilgrimage, charity, marriage and divorce, debts. It holds the verse usually counted the longest in the Qur'an, about writing down a loan, and Ayat al-Kursi, the Throne Verse. Near its end, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith in Muslim: don't make your houses into graveyards; Satan flees from a house in which Surah al-Baqarah is recited. The shortest is al-Kawthar, Surah 108. Al-'Asr and an-Nasr also have three verses, but al-Kawthar's three are the shortest of all. You met it in camp four. "Lo! We have given thee Abundance;" then: so pray to your Lord, and sacrifice. Then: the one who hates you is the one cut off. Reports say it came at a hard time, when the Prophet's sons had died young and an enemy mocked him as cut off, a man with no line. Three verses to answer a grief. A surah's weight isn't its length. Al-Kawthar is a whole surah, as complete as al-Baqarah. The Qur'an's challenge, made in al-Baqarah itself, is to bring a surah like it, and it names no length. Both open with the same bismillah.
screen: `AL-BAQARAH: 286 VERSES` · `A HOUSE WHERE IT'S RECITED` · `AL-KAWTHAR: THREE VERSES` · `WEIGHT ISN'T LENGTH`

segments.voice: If you know al-Kawthar, say it now, slowly, all three verses, bismillah first; if you don't, remember it in English: abundance; pray and sacrifice; the one cut off. Then stay with the first verse only, abundance, and let one thing you've been given but forget to count come to mind. If another comes, let it join the first.

326.title: Who is speaking
326.hook: Allah speaks as I, We and He, and the shifts carry meaning
326.howItsDone: Students of the Qur'an learn to notice its shifts of voice, from We to I to He and the command 'say', and teachers often point to the turn in al-Fatiha as the first example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the longest and the shortest: al-Baqarah's two hundred eighty-six verses, al-Kawthar's three. Your line was long and short.

Listen to a good wedding speech. The best man talks about the groom: he's loyal, he's always late, he once drove four hours to fix a friend's sink. He, and he, and he. Then he turns to face him: and you, I'm proud of you. The whole room feels the shift. Back on day fifteen, inside the Fatiha, you met the same turn: four lines about God, then suddenly, Thee alone we worship. Today that turn gets its name, and it turns out to be everywhere in the Qur'an.
screen: `HE, AND HE, AND HE.` → `THEN, SUDDENLY: YOU.` → `WHO IS SPEAKING?`

segments.voice: That sudden turn has a name in Arabic rhetoric: iltifat, a turning, a shift of person. The Qur'an does it again and again, and it's part of what makes it feel alive, even startling, the first time you notice. In Pickthall's rendering of the Fatiha: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help." Scholars say it's as if, after praising, the one praying has come near enough to speak face to face. Across the Qur'an, God speaks in more than one way. Very often as We: We sent down, We created. In Arabic this is the plural of majesty, the way a sovereign speaks, and Muslims understand it as grandeur, never as more than one God. The Qur'an is fierce about that oneness: Say, He is Allah, the One. God also speaks as I, and those moments are often the most intimate. In Pickthall's words: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh." Not We: I. Close. And God is spoken of as He, in the third person, as in much of the Fatiha. Then there's another voice: the Prophet ﷺ being told what to say. That's the small word qul, say, at the start of al-Ikhlas and the other quls you met on day two hundred twenty-seven, the word Muslims keep when they recite. The Prophet isn't the author; he's being handed the words. Scholars treat these shifts as meaningful: We for power and creation, I for nearness and mercy, He for praise and description, say for the words passed on. Not every turn has an agreed explanation. But listening for who is speaking, and to whom, changes how a verse lands.
screen: `THE TURN IN THE FATIHA` · `WE: THE PLURAL OF MAJESTY` · `I: THE MOST INTIMATE` · `QUL: THE PROPHET IS TOLD TO SAY`

segments.voice: Take al-Ikhlas, say, He is Allah, the One, and ask slowly: who is speaking, to whom, about whom? God, telling the Prophet, and through him everyone, about God, as He. Then say the Fatiha's praise, pause, say Thee alone we worship, and notice where your attention turns.
Iltifat. A turning, a shift of person — the Qur'an's sudden switch between We, I, He and say that one notices once pointed out. Today's word.
Your line: listen for who is speaking. When a voice turns to you, something usually changes. Until tomorrow.

327.title: Handling the mushaf
327.hook: many keep it high, clean, and touch it only in wudu
327.howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it on a high, clean shelf with nothing on top, read it on a stand, and bury or respectfully dispose of worn-out copies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, iltifat: who is speaking, We, I, He, and say. Your line was listen for who is speaking.

Look for the Qur'an in a Muslim family's home. You probably won't find it on the floor, under a pile of magazines, or on the bottom shelf beside the shoes. It'll be up high, often wrapped in cloth, sometimes on a shelf by itself. A grandmother may kiss it before she opens it. A child may be told never to put anything on top of it.
screen: `NOT ON THE FLOOR.` → `UP HIGH, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `NOTHING ON TOP OF IT.`

segments.voice: These customs come from how Muslims regard the Qur'an: the speech of God, written down. The written copy, the mushaf, is treated with the honor due to what it carries. One rule is about touching it. Surah 56 describes the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, as a book "Which none toucheth save the purified". Scholars read that verse in more than one way; some commentators understand it to be about the preserved book in heaven, touched only by angels. Still, the four Sunni schools of law hold, as a rule, that a person should be in a state of purity, with wudu, to touch the Arabic mushaf. They also point to a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to Yemen, recorded in the Muwatta of Imam Malik: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. Some scholars held otherwise, and there are discussions about children who are learning, about translations, and about phones and apps, which some scholars say aren't a mushaf in the same sense. Beyond the rules there's a whole culture of care. A folding wooden stand holds it open so it doesn't lie on the floor. It often sits on the highest shelf, with nothing on top. People avoid taking it into a bathroom. A worn-out copy isn't thrown in the trash: it's buried, or respectfully burned, or placed in special boxes that some mosques keep. Some Muslims kiss it; others say no such practice is required, and simply handle it with care. What the customs share is simple: this isn't an ordinary book, so it doesn't get an ordinary place.
screen: `NONE TOUCHETH SAVE THE PURIFIED` · `THE SCHOOLS: TOUCH IT WITH WUDU` · `A STAND, A HIGH SHELF, NOTHING ON TOP` · `WORN COPIES ARE BURIED, NOT TRASHED`

segments.voice: If there's a mushaf or a translation in your home, picture where it sits right now, and whether it has a clean, high place with nothing stacked on it. If you don't have one, think of the book or object you treat most carefully, and why, and notice what it feels like to honor something. If you pray, you might make wudu before you next open it.

328.title: Khatm: the whole book
328.hook: finishing a whole reading, often in Ramadan, with a gathering
328.howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a full reading of the Qur'an in Ramadan, at home or through the tarawih prayers, and mosques and families often mark a khatm with a gathering, a special supplication and food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, handling the mushaf: purity to touch it, a high place, never the trash. Your line was keep it high.

It's late on one of the last nights of Ramadan. The mosque is fuller than it's been all month. Children are awake long past their bedtimes. The imam is reciting An-Nas, the very last surah, and in some mosques, when he finishes, he goes straight back and recites the opening of the book again. Then comes a long supplication. Some people are weeping; others are already handing out sweets. The whole book, finished.
screen: `A LATE NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `THE LAST SURAH, THEN THE FIRST.` → `WEEPING, AND SWEETS.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a seal, a finishing. It's the same root as khatam, seal, in the title the Qur'an gives the Prophet ﷺ in Surah 33: the seal of the prophets. For the Qur'an, a khatm is one complete reading, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas. Ramadan is its season. The hadith collections say the angel Jibril went over the whole Qur'an with the Prophet every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. So Ramadan is when a full reading is most often attempted, alone at home, or by hearing it across the nights of tarawih, often a juz' a night. When a mosque reaches the end, there's often a gathering, with a special supplication after the last surah, the du'a of khatm, often long and often tearful. A report says the companion Anas ibn Malik, when he finished the Qur'an, would gather his family and make du'a with them. Customs vary. In some places a child's first khatm is celebrated with a party and new clothes: in parts of South Asia it's called an Ameen, in Turkey a hatim. And some readers who finish An-Nas begin again at once from al-Fatiha, so the reading never really stops. How often? You met one hadith in the week of the thirty parts: once a month, and not faster than seven days. Another says the one who finishes in less than three days hasn't understood it. So speed isn't the point. A page a day is slow, and it still arrives. The point is the whole: not only the parts you love, but every page, once.
screen: `KHATM: A SEAL, A FINISHING` · `RAMADAN IS ITS SEASON` · `A GATHERING, A SUPPLICATION` · `BEGIN AGAIN FROM AL-FATIHA`

segments.voice: Ask what pace is true for you: a juz' a day, a page a day, a few verses a day, or one reciter heard through the whole book. Pick an amount you could keep on a bad day, not only a good one, and hold that plan quietly. If you're here to learn about the path rather than practice it, choose a translation of the meanings and a pace.
Khatm. A seal: one complete reading of the Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, often finished in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, once. However long it takes, the whole book arrives. See you tomorrow.

329.title: Heard in the world
329.hook: from Jakarta to Dakar, the same Arabic is recited every day
329.howItsDone: The daily prayers are recited in Arabic whatever language a Muslim speaks at home, and many regions have their own well-known reciters and styles of recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khatm: the whole book, sealed, and begun again. Your line was the whole book, once. Day three hundred twenty-nine, the end of a week.

Dawn is a moving line. Right now it's reaching a new strip of the earth, and somewhere in that strip, someone is standing to pray and reciting al-Fatiha. An hour from now the line will have moved west, and someone else will be saying the same seven verses in the same Arabic. Follow the dawn around the planet and you'll hear the Qur'an recited in every time zone.
screen: `DAWN IS A MOVING LINE.` → `THE SAME SEVEN VERSES.` → `EVERY TIME ZONE.`

segments.voice: Demographers put the number of Muslims near two billion, and most of them are not Arabs. Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country. Muslims speak a great many languages at home, from Javanese to Hausa to Bosnian to English. Yet the five daily prayers are said in the same Arabic: a child in Jakarta and a grandmother in Dakar recite the Fatiha in the same sounds. The Qur'an names that variety as a sign. In Pickthall's words: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Different tongues, one recitation. And each place has its own sound. Egypt's twentieth-century reciters, heard on the radio, carried a long, melodic style far beyond Egypt. Imams in the Gulf are often heard in a plainer, flowing style. In Morocco you may hear the reading of Warsh, met last week. Indonesia and Malaysia hold national recitation competitions, where young men and women recite before large crowds. Turkish reciters have their own ornamented tradition. Same words, different voices, and this week showed why that holds together. The hafiz carries it by heart. The sajdah verses bring a room to the floor. The longest and the shortest, al-Baqarah and al-Kawthar. Iltifat, who is speaking: We, I, He, and say. The mushaf, handled with care. Khatm, the whole book. And now the whole world, reciting it.
screen: `NEAR TWO BILLION, MOSTLY NOT ARABS` · `ONE ARABIC, FIVE TIMES A DAY` · `YOUR LANGUAGES AND COLORS: A SIGN` · `EACH PLACE HAS ITS OWN SOUND`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture that line of dawn moving across the earth, and along it, voice after voice, in the same words; if you recite, let your voice be one of them. Another time, play a recitation from somewhere you've never been: an Indonesian competition, a West African reciter in Warsh, an Egyptian master from the radio years.
Al-'Alamin. The worlds — as in rabb al-'alamin, Lord of the worlds, the same Arabic recited from Jakarta to Dakar. Today's word.
Your line: the same words everywhere. The difference of your languages is a sign. And that closes the week.
